title: Do Trained Agents Steer Back? Measuring Recovery from Mistakes in Atari Agents Against Their Own Blind Replay
content: A trained agent will sometimes press a wrong button. A noisy controller, a delayed input or an attacker can force this. We ask a simple question: when this happens, does the agent bring itself back on track, or does it only carry on as if nothing happened? To answer it, we force ("kick") an Atari agent into a different action for a short time. From the exact same kicked emulator state, we then run two copies of the game. In one copy the agent is in control again. In the other copy, the agent's original button presses are replayed blind. The difference in how often each copy loses an extra life is the steer-back index (SBI). The Atari emulator is deterministic, so this comparison is exact. We add built-in controls: a "null" kick that must change nothing, an exact replay check, and a hand-written controller that must show steer-back. We measure 38 published agents (PPO, A2C, DQN and QR-DQN on 10 games). We also measure PPO agents at 10 checkpoints of training, for 3 games and 2 seeds. We find three things. (1) Steer-back is common: 30 of 38 agents recover clearly better than their own blind replay. (2) Within a game, agents with a higher score steer back more, but the algorithm family matters little. (3) During training, recovery and skill are separate abilities. In Breakout, recovery appears first: after 1M steps it has reached more than half of its final level, while the score has reached only about 5% of its final level. In Seaquest, recovery jumps up at the same moment as the score, in both seeds, even though this moment comes at a different time in each seed. In Asteroids, the score keeps rising but steer-back never rises above zero, and it drifts below zero by the end of training.
